claim: Congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (CHH) is characterized by absent puberty and infertility due to gonadotropin releasing hormone (GnRH) deficiency.
source: Congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (CHH) is a condition characterized by absent puberty and infertility due to gonadotropin releasing hormone (GnRH) deficiency, which is often associated with anosmia (Kallmann syndrome, KS).
evidence: This is a definitional statement about CHH that is supported by established scientific knowledge and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: CHH is often associated with anosmia (Kallmann syndrome, KS).
source: Congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (CHH) is a condition characterized by absent puberty and infertility due to gonadotropin releasing hormone (GnRH) deficiency, which is often associated with anosmia (Kallmann syndrome, KS).
evidence: This is a well-established clinical association supported by scientific knowledge.

claim: Loss-of-function heterozygous mutations in AMH and AMHR2 were identified in 3% of CHH probands using whole-exome sequencing.
source: We identified loss-of-function heterozygous mutations in anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) and its receptor, AMHR2, in 3% of CHH probands using whole-exome sequencing.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from whole-exome sequencing of 136 CHH patients, identifying 4 patients with mutations.

claim: AMH is expressed in migratory GnRH neurons during embryonic development in both mouse and human fetuses.
source: We showed that during embryonic development, AMH is expressed in migratory GnRH neurons in both mouse and human fetuses and unconvered a novel function of AMH as a pro-motility factor for GnRH neurons.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data including FACS-isolated GnRH neurons, nasal explants, and immunofluorescence in human fetuses shown in Figure 1.

claim: AMH functions as a pro-motility factor for GnRH neurons.
source: We showed that during embryonic development, AMH is expressed in migratory GnRH neurons in both mouse and human fetuses and unconvered a novel function of AMH as a pro-motility factor for GnRH neurons.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from transwell migration assays showing AMH increases GN11 cell motility (Figure 5).

claim: Amhr2-deficient mice show abnormal development of the peripheral olfactory system.
source: Pathohistological analysis of Amhr2-deficient mice showed abnormal development of the peripheral olfactory system and defective embryonic migration of the neuroendocrine GnRH cells to the basal forebrain, which results in reduced fertility in adults.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from in utero injections with Amhr2 neutralizing antibody and genetic knockout mice shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Amhr2-deficient mice show defective embryonic migration of GnRH cells to the basal forebrain.
source: Pathohistological analysis of Amhr2-deficient mice showed abnormal development of the peripheral olfactory system and defective embryonic migration of the neuroendocrine GnRH cells to the basal forebrain, which results in reduced fertility in adults.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing accumulation of GnRH cells in the nasal compartment and reduced numbers in the ventral forebrain in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Amhr2-deficient mice have reduced fertility in adulthood.
source: Pathohistological analysis of Amhr2-deficient mice showed abnormal development of the peripheral olfactory system and defective embryonic migration of the neuroendocrine GnRH cells to the basal forebrain, which results in reduced fertility in adults.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from fertility tests showing reduced litters, pups per litter, and delayed first litter in Figure 4n.

claim: AMH signaling insufficiency contributes to the pathogenesis of CHH in humans.
source: Our findings highlight a novel role for AMH in the development and function of GnRH neurons and indicate that AMH signaling insufficiency contributes to the pathogenesis of CHH in humans.
evidence: This is supported by the identification of loss-of-function mutations in AMH and AMHR2 in CHH patients and functional validation showing these mutations impair GnRH neuron migration and secretion.

claim: GnRH is essential for puberty onset and reproduction.
source: Gonadotropin releasing hormone (GnRH) is essential for puberty onset and reproduction.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the role of GnRH in the reproductive axis.

claim: GnRH is released into the pituitary portal blood vessels for delivery to the anterior pituitary.
source: GnRH is released into the pituitary portal blood vessels for delivery to the anterior pituitary.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about GnRH physiology, supported by citation to Christian and Moenter, 2010.

claim: GnRH controls the production and release of LH and FSH in the anterior pituitary.
source: There, GnRH controls the production and release of the gonadotropins LH (luteinizing hormone) and FSH (follicle stimulating hormone), which in turn stimulate gametogenesis and sex steroid production in the gonads (Christian and Moenter, 2010).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, supported by citation.

claim: LH and FSH stimulate gametogenesis and sex steroid production in the gonads.
source: There, GnRH controls the production and release of the gonadotropins LH (luteinizing hormone) and FSH (follicle stimulating hormone), which in turn stimulate gametogenesis and sex steroid production in the gonads (Christian and Moenter, 2010).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about gonadotropin function, supported by citation.

claim: GnRH-secreting neurons originate in the nasal placode outside the central nervous system during embryonic development.
source: GnRH–secreting neurons are unusual neuroendocrine cells, as they originate in the nasal placode outside the central nervous system during embryonic development, and migrate to the hypothalamus along the vomeronasal and terminal nerves (VNN, TN) (Wray et al., 1989; Schwanzel-Fukuda and Pfaff, 1989).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about GnRH neuron development, supported by citations to Wray et al., 1989 and Schwanzel-Fukuda and Pfaff, 1989.

claim: GnRH neurons migrate to the hypothalamus along the vomeronasal and terminal nerves.
source: GnRH–secreting neurons are unusual neuroendocrine cells, as they originate in the nasal placode outside the central nervous system during embryonic development, and migrate to the hypothalamus along the vomeronasal and terminal nerves (VNN, TN) (Wray et al., 1989; Schwanzel-Fukuda and Pfaff, 1989).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about GnRH neuron migration, supported by citations.

claim: The GnRH neuronal migration process is evolutionarily conserved and follows a similar spatio-temporal pattern in all mammals.
source: This process is evolutionarily conserved and follows a similar spatio-temporal pattern in all mammals (Wray et al., 1989; Schwanzel-Fukuda and Pfaff, 1989), including humans (Schwanzel-Fukuda et al., 1996; Casoni et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies showing conservation across species.

claim: Disruption of GnRH neuronal migration and/or defective GnRH synthesis and secretion leads to congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.
source: Disruption of GnRH neuronal migration and/or defective GnRH synthesis and secretion leads to congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadisms (CHH), a rare endocrine disorder (prevalence: 1 in 4000) characterized by absent or incomplete puberty resulting in infertility (Boehm et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about CHH pathogenesis, supported by citation to Boehm et al., 2015.

claim: CHH has a prevalence of 1 in 4000.
source: Disruption of GnRH neuronal migration and/or defective GnRH synthesis and secretion leads to congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadisms (CHH), a rare endocrine disorder (prevalence: 1 in 4000) characterized by absent or incomplete puberty resulting in infertility (Boehm et al., 2015).
evidence: This prevalence data is supported by citation to Boehm et al., 2015.

claim: CHH is clinically and genetically heterogeneous.
source: CHH is clinically and genetically heterogeneous with several causal genes identified to date (Boehm et al., 2015), and follows various modes of transmission, including oligogenic inheritance (Sykiotis et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies documenting the heterogeneity of CHH.

claim: CHH follows various modes of transmission, including oligogenic inheritance.
source: CHH is clinically and genetically heterogeneous with several causal genes identified to date (Boehm et al., 2015), and follows various modes of transmission, including oligogenic inheritance (Sykiotis et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sykiotis et al., 2010 documenting oligogenic inheritance.

claim: Mutations identified so far only account for half of clinically reported CHH cases.
source: However, the mutations identified so far only account for half of clinically reported cases, suggesting that other causal genes remain to be discovered.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the genetic landscape of CHH.

claim: AMH is a TGF-β family member.
source: AMH is a TGF-β family member and it signals by binding to a specific type II receptor (AMHR2) (di Clemente et al., 1994; Baarends et al., 1994), which heterodimerizes with one of several type I TGF-β receptors (Acvr1 [Alk2], Bmpr1a [Alk3] and Bmpr1b [Alk6]), to recruit Smad proteins that subsequently undergo nuclear translocation to regulate target gene expression (Josso and Clemente, 2003).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about AMH, supported by citations.

claim: AMH signals by binding to AMHR2, which heterodimerizes with type I TGF-β receptors to recruit Smad proteins.
source: AMH is a TGF-β family member and it signals by binding to a specific type II receptor (AMHR2) (di Clemente et al., 1994; Baarends et al., 1994), which heterodimerizes with one of several type I TGF-β receptors (Acvr1 [Alk2], Bmpr1a [Alk3] and Bmpr1b [Alk6]), to recruit Smad proteins that subsequently undergo nuclear translocation to regulate target gene expression (Josso and Clemente, 2003).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about AMH signaling, supported by citations.

claim: AMH signaling has been traditionally reported to play a crucial role during sex differentiation and gonadal functions.
source: Although AMH signaling has been traditionally reported to play a crucial role during sex differentiation and gonadal functions (Josso et al., 1998; Behringer et al., 1994), accumulating evidence has started to shed light on unexpected functions of AMH in the central nervous system as well as in the pituitary (Lebeurrier et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2009; Tata et al., 2018; Cimino et al., 2016; Garrel et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations to Josso et al., 1998 and Behringer et al., 1994.

claim: AMH has functions in the central nervous system and pituitary.
source: Although AMH signaling has been traditionally reported to play a crucial role during sex differentiation and gonadal functions (Josso et al., 1998; Behringer et al., 1994), accumulating evidence has started to shed light on unexpected functions of AMH in the central nervous system as well as in the pituitary (Lebeurrier et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2009; Tata et al., 2018; Cimino et al., 2016; Garrel et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies documenting CNS and pituitary functions of AMH.

claim: GnRH neurons express AMHR2 from early fetal development to adulthood.
source: We have previously shown that GnRH neurons express AMHR2 from early fetal development to adulthood and that AMH stimulates GnRH neuronal activity and hormone secretion in mature GnRH cells (Cimino et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors (Cimino et al., 2016).

claim: AMH stimulates GnRH neuronal activity and hormone secretion in mature GnRH cells.
source: We have previously shown that GnRH neurons express AMHR2 from early fetal development to adulthood and that AMH stimulates GnRH neuronal activity and hormone secretion in mature GnRH cells (Cimino et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors (Cimino et al., 2016).

claim: Pharmacological or genetic invalidation of Amhr2 signaling in vivo alters GnRH migration.
source: Finally, we show that pharmacological or genetic invalidation of Amhr2 signaling in vivo alters GnRH migration and the projections of VNN/TN to the basal forebrain, which results in a reduced size of this neuronal population in adult brains, altered ovulation and fertility.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from in utero injections and Amhr2 knockout mice shown in Figures 2, 3, and 4.

claim: Pharmacological or genetic invalidation of Amhr2 signaling alters the projections of VNN/TN to the basal forebrain.
source: Finally, we show that pharmacological or genetic invalidation of Amhr2 signaling in vivo alters GnRH migration and the projections of VNN/TN to the basal forebrain, which results in a reduced size of this neuronal population in adult brains, altered ovulation and fertility.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing abnormal peripherin-positive fiber projections in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Invalidation of Amhr2 signaling results in a reduced size of the GnRH neuronal population in adult brains.
source: Finally, we show that pharmacological or genetic invalidation of Amhr2 signaling in vivo alters GnRH migration and the projections of VNN/TN to the basal forebrain, which results in a reduced size of this neuronal population in adult brains, altered ovulation and fertility.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing 40% reduction in GnRH cell number in Amhr2-/- mice in Figure 4i.

claim: Invalidation of Amhr2 signaling results in altered ovulation and fertility.
source: Finally, we show that pharmacological or genetic invalidation of Amhr2 signaling in vivo alters GnRH migration and the projections of VNN/TN to the basal forebrain, which results in a reduced size of this neuronal population in adult brains, altered ovulation and fertility.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing reduced corpora lutea and impaired fertility in Amhr2-/- mice in Figure 4k and 4n.

claim: Four heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in AMH and AMHR2 were identified among 136 CHH patients.
source: The involvement of the AMH signaling pathway in GnRH ontogeny and secretion led to the identification of four heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in AMH and AMHR2 among 136 CHH patients.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from whole-exome sequencing and functional validation shown in Figures 6 and 7 and Table 1.

claim: Amh is expressed by GnRH migratory cells at E12.5 in mice.
source: These experiments revealed expression of Amh already at E12.5 both in GnRH neurons and in total head extracts (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from FACS-isolated GnRH neurons and RT-PCR shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Amh expression in GnRH neurons increases from early embryonic development (E12.5) to adult life (PN90).
source: Moreover, real-time PCR experiments showed increasing expression of Amh in GnRH neurons from early embryonic development (E12.5) to adult life (PN90; Figure 1a,b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from quantitative RT-PCR shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Amh is expressed in punctated structures resembling vesicles in migratory GnRH neurons in nasal explants.
source: These experiments revealed the presence of Amh-immunoreactivity in punctated structures resembling vesicles (arrowheads in Figure 1e,f) in migratory neurons.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data from nasal explants shown in Figure 1d-f.

claim: AMH is expressed in GnRH neurons but not on vomeronasal/terminal nerves in GW11 human fetuses.
source: Triple-immunofluorescence staining of coronal sections of GW11 fetuses (n = 2 females) revealed that AMH is expressed in GnRH neurons but not on the vomeronasal/terminal nerves (TAG-1-positive) that form the migratory scaffold for GnRH neurons (Figure 1h–k).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data from human fetal sections shown in Figure 1h-k.

claim: At GW11, the only neurons expressing AMH in the forebrain are GnRH neuroendocrine cells.
source: Interestingly, at this developmental stage the only neurons expressing AMH in the forebrain were the GnRH neuroendocrine cells (Figure 1m–o).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data from human fetal forebrain sections shown in Figure 1m-o.

claim: Acute pharmacological blockade of Amhr2 with a neutralizing antibody affects the development of the olfactory, vomeronasal and terminal systems.
source: This was achieved by in utero injection of Amhr2-NA delivered into the olfactory pit of E12.5 embryos at the beginning of the migratory process, and subsequent analysis of GnRH migration and its axonal scaffold 48 hr later (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from in utero injections showing abnormal ON/VNN development in Figure 2.

claim: Amhr2 neutralization has no effect on GnRH neuron survival at E14.5.
source: At E14.5, the total number of GnRH neurons was comparable between control and Amhr2-NA-treated embryos (Figure 2g), indicating that Amhr2 neutralization had no effect on GnRH neuron survival.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing no difference in total GnRH cell number in Figure 2g.

claim: Amhr2 neutralization causes accumulation of GnRH cells in the nasal compartment and decreased cell numbers in the ventral forebrain.
source: However, a significant accumulation of GnRH cells in the nasal compartment, concomitant to decreased cell numbers within the vFB, is suggestive of a delayed GnRH cell migration in Amhr2-NA injected embryos (Figure 2h).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing altered GnRH cell distribution in Figure 2h.

claim: In Amhr2-/- embryos at E13.5, olfactory axons only partially innervate the olfactory bulb.
source: In Amhr2+/+ embryos, peripherin-positive fibers were seen to innervate almost completely the OB (Figure 3b, f, h and j, arrowheads), whereas in Amhr2-/- mice olfactory axons only partially innervated their target tissues (Figure 3c, g, i and k, arrowheads).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from iDISCO and light sheet microscopy shown in Figure 3.

claim: In Amhr2-/- embryos at E13.5, GnRH neurons appear more clustered in the nasal compartment and fewer reach the ventral forebrain.
source: Moreover, whereas in Amhr2+/+ embryos GnRH neurons entered the brain along the TN projections and migrated to the ventral forebrain (vFB; Figure 3d and j, arrows), in Amhr2-/- embryos GnRH neurons appeared more clustered in the nasal compartment, stuck in proximity to the VNO, and fewer GnRH cells reached the vFB at this embryonic stage (Figure 3e and k, arrows).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from iDISCO and light sheet microscopy shown in Figure 3.

claim: Adult Amhr2-/- mice have a 40% reduction in GnRH cell number compared to wild-type mice.
source: When we counted the total number of GnRH-positive cells in Amhr2+/+, Amhr2+/- and Amhr2-/- female brains, we found no difference between wild type and heterozygous mice, while we observed a significant 40% reduction in GnRH cell number in Amhr2-/- mice as compared to the other genotypes (Figure 4i).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from GnRH cell counting in adult brains shown in Figure 4i.

claim: Male and female Amhr2-/- mice show similar GnRH cell loss compared to sex-matched wild-type littermates.
source: Male and female homozygous animals showed a similar GnRH cell loss as compared to sex-matched wild-type littermates (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Circulating LH is significantly lower in Amhr2+/- and Amhr2-/- adult female mice compared to wild-type littermates.
source: Circulating LH was found to be significantly lower in Amhr2+/- and Amhr2-/- animals as compared to wild-type littermates (Figure 4j), supporting an impairment of GnRH secretion in these animals.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from LH measurements shown in Figure 4j.

claim: Only Amhr2-/- mice exhibit reduced ovulation as shown by fewer corpora lutea.
source: However, only Amhr2-/- mice exhibited reduced ovulation, as shown by the presence of fewer post-ovulation corpora lutea in the ovaries of Amhr2-/- mice as compared to Amhr2+/- and wild-type animals (Figure 4k).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from ovarian histology shown in Figure 4k.

claim: Both Amhr2+/- and Amhr2-/- female mice have significantly lower LH pulse frequency compared to wild-type littermates.
source: We then evaluated LH pulsatility by serial blood sampling in female diestrous mice (Figure 4l,m) and found that both Amhr2+/- and Amhr2-/- animals had a significantly lower LH pulse frequency as compared to wild-type littermates.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from LH pulsatility measurements shown in Figure 4l and 4m.

claim: Amhr2-/- and Amhr2+/- females show significant impairment of fertility.
source: We found a significant impairement of fertility in both Amhr2-/- and Amhr2+/- females, as indicated by fewer litters per months, by fewer pups per litter and by a significant delay in the first litter after pairing as compared to Amhr2+/+ females (Figure 4n).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from fertility tests shown in Figure 4n.

claim: Heterozygous Amhr2+/- females display an intermediate fertility phenotype between Amhr2+/+ and Amhr2-/- mice.
source: Heterozygous females displayed an intermediate phenotype between Amhr2+/+ and Amhr2-/- mice, since all fertility measurements revealed statistically significant differences between Amhr2+/- and Amhr2+/+ mice and between Amhr2+/- and Amhr2-/- mice (Figure 4n).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from fertility tests shown in Figure 4n.

claim: In heterozygous Amhr2+/- males, only the number of litters/90 days is significantly reduced compared to Amhr2+/+ males.
source: In heterozygous males, only the number of litters/90 days was found to be significantly reduced as compared to Amhr2+/+ males (Figure 4n).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from fertility tests shown in Figure 4n.

claim: Amhr2-/- males are completely infertile.
source: Amhr2-/- males are completely infertile (Figure 4n), in agreement with previous reports showing that inactivation of Amhr2 or Amh in humans and mice leads to persistent Müllerian duct syndrome (Imbeaud et al., 1995; Mishina et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from fertility tests shown in Figure 4n and citations to previous studies.

claim: Inactivation of Amhr2 or Amh in humans and mice leads to persistent Müllerian duct syndrome.
source: Amhr2-/- males are completely infertile (Figure 4n), in agreement with previous reports showing that inactivation of Amhr2 or Amh in humans and mice leads to persistent Müllerian duct syndrome (Imbeaud et al., 1995; Mishina et al., 1996).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations to Imbeaud et al., 1995 and Mishina et al., 1996.

claim: Both GN11 and GT1-7 cells express Amh and Amhr2.
source: Our data show that both GN11 and GT1-7 cells express Amh and Amhr2, even though the transcript levels were significantly higher in GT1-7 cells as compared to GN11 cells (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from RT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Amh and Amhr2 transcript levels are significantly higher in GT1-7 cells compared to GN11 cells.
source: Our data show that both GN11 and GT1-7 cells express Amh and Amhr2, even though the transcript levels were significantly higher in GT1-7 cells as compared to GN11 cells (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from RT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Both GN11 and GT1-7 cells express Acvr1 and Bmpr1a, with GT1-7 cells displaying higher levels of expression.
source: As for the Amh-type one receptors, both cell lines express Acvr1 and Bmpr1a, with GT1-7 cells displaying higher levels of expression compared to GN1 cells (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from RT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 5a.

claim: GN11 cells, but not GT1-7 cells, express Bmpr1b.
source: Interestingly, GN11 cells, but not GT1-7 cells, express Bmpr1b (Figure 5a), indicating that Amhr2/Bmpr1b signaling maybe a putative hallmark of migratory GnRH neurons.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from RT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Amhr2/Bmpr1b signaling may be a putative hallmark of migratory GnRH neurons.
source: Interestingly, GN11 cells, but not GT1-7 cells, express Bmpr1b (Figure 5a), indicating that Amhr2/Bmpr1b signaling maybe a putative hallmark of migratory GnRH neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential expression of Bmpr1b in GN11 (migratory) versus GT1-7 (post-migratory) cells.

claim: AMH significantly increases the phosphorylation of ERK1/2 in GN11 cells in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Here, we found that AMH, at concentrations previously reported to be functional in other cell lines (Garrel et al., 2016), significantly increased the phosphorylation of ERK1/2 in GN11 cells in a dose- and time-dependent manner (Figure 5b,c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Western blot analysis shown in Figure 5b and 5c.

claim: AMH significantly increases the phosphorylation of ERK1/2 in GN11 cells in a time-dependent manner.
source: Here, we found that AMH, at concentrations previously reported to be functional in other cell lines (Garrel et al., 2016), significantly increased the phosphorylation of ERK1/2 in GN11 cells in a dose- and time-dependent manner (Figure 5b,c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Western blot analysis shown in Figure 5b and 5c.

claim: AMH-dependent activation of MAPK pathway is prevented by pharmacological blockage of Amhr2.
source: The AMH-dependent activation of MAPK pathway was prevented by the pharmacological blockage of Amhr2 (AMHR2 neutralizing antibody; AMHR2-NA; Figure 5b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Western blot analysis shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Recombinant human AMH significantly increases the motility of GN11 cells at doses of 50, 100, and 250 ng/ml.
source: Using transwell assays, we showed that recombinant human AMH was able to significantly increase the motility of GN11 cells at all tested doses (50 ng/ml; 100 ng/ml; 250 ng/ml) compared to controls (serum-free medium, SFM; Figure 5d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from transwell migration assays shown in Figure 5d.

claim: AMH-dependent induction of GN11 cell motility is prevented by the MAPK pathway inhibitor U0126.
source: In agreement with our biochemical results (Figure 5b,c), the AMH-dependent induction of cell motility was prevented by the selective pharmacological antagonist of MAPK pathway (U0126 inhibits MEKK1, the upstream activator of ERK) and by AMHR2-NA (Figure 5d,e).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from transwell migration assays shown in Figure 5d and 5e.

claim: AMH-dependent induction of GN11 cell motility is prevented by AMHR2 neutralizing antibody.
source: In agreement with our biochemical results (Figure 5b,c), the AMH-dependent induction of cell motility was prevented by the selective pharmacological antagonist of MAPK pathway (U0126 inhibits MEKK1, the upstream activator of ERK) and by AMHR2-NA (Figure 5d,e).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from transwell migration assays shown in Figure 5d and 5e.

claim: Knockdown of Amhr2 results in significantly reduced GN11 cell motility in response to AMH.
source: In contrast, knockdown of Amhr2 and Bmpr1b resulted in significantly reduced GN11 cell motility in response to AMH as compared to the control groups (mock and siRNA-NC transfected cells; Figure 5g).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from transwell migration assays with siRNA knockdown shown in Figure 5g.

claim: Knockdown of Bmpr1b results in significantly reduced GN11 cell motility in response to AMH.
source: In contrast, knockdown of Amhr2 and Bmpr1b resulted in significantly reduced GN11 cell motility in response to AMH as compared to the control groups (mock and siRNA-NC transfected cells; Figure 5g).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from transwell migration assays with siRNA knockdown shown in Figure 5g.

claim: AMH promotes GN11 cell motility through the Amhr2/Bmpr1b receptor complex and activation of the MAPK intracellular pathway.
source: These data show that AMH promotes GN11 cell motility through the Amhr2/Bmpr1b receptor complex and activation of the MAPK intracellular pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data from receptor knockdown and MAPK inhibition experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Three probands from European descent harbor heterozygous missense mutations in AMH (p.Thr99Ser, p.Pro151Ser, and p.Asp238Glu).
source: In this study, we performed whole exome sequencing in 75 KS and 61 normosmic CHH (nCHH) probands who did not harbor pathogenic mutations in known CHH genes, and identified in three probands from European descent heterozygous missense mutations in AMH (Table 1, Figure 6a,b). These mutations (p.Thr99Ser, p.Pro151Ser, and p.Asp238Glu) lie in the N-terminal pro-protein domain (Figure 6a), and all affected amino acids were highly conserved across species (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from whole-exome sequencing shown in Table 1 and Figure 6.

claim: The AMH mutations p.Thr99Ser, p.Pro151Ser, and p.Asp238Glu lie in the N-terminal pro-protein domain.
source: In this study, we performed whole exome sequencing in 75 KS and 61 normosmic CHH (nCHH) probands who did not harbor pathogenic mutations in known CHH genes, and identified in three probands from European descent heterozygous missense mutations in AMH (Table 1, Figure 6a,b). These mutations (p.Thr99Ser, p.Pro151Ser, and p.Asp238Glu) lie in the N-terminal pro-protein domain (Figure 6a), and all affected amino acids were highly conserved across species (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is supported by the schematic representation of AMH protein structure shown in Figure 6a.

claim: The amino acids affected by AMH mutations (Thr99, Pro151, Asp238) are highly conserved across species.
source: In this study, we performed whole exome sequencing in 75 KS and 61 normosmic CHH (nCHH) probands who did not harbor pathogenic mutations in known CHH genes, and identified in three probands from European descent heterozygous missense mutations in AMH (Table 1, Figure 6a,b). These mutations (p.Thr99Ser, p.Pro151Ser, and p.Asp238Glu) lie in the N-terminal pro-protein domain (Figure 6a), and all affected amino acids were highly conserved across species (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: One female with normosmic CHH harbors a heterozygous in-frame 27-nucleotide deletion in AMHR2 (p.Gly445_Leu453del).
source: Additionally, one female with normosmic CHH (nCHH) harbors a heterozygous in-frame 27-nucleotide deletion in AMHR2. This p.Gly445_Leu453del deletion lies within the catalytic intracellular serine/threonine domain of the receptor (Figure 6d–6f).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from whole-exome sequencing shown in Figure 6d-f.

claim: The AMHR2 p.Gly445_Leu453del deletion lies within the catalytic intracellular serine/threonine kinase domain of the receptor.
source: Additionally, one female with normosmic CHH (nCHH) harbors a heterozygous in-frame 27-nucleotide deletion in AMHR2. This p.Gly445_Leu453del deletion lies within the catalytic intracellular serine/threonine domain of the receptor (Figure 6d–6f).
evidence: This is supported by the schematic representation of AMHR2 protein structure shown in Figure 6d.

claim: All three AMH mutants (p.Pro151Ser, p.Asp238Glu, and p.Thr99Ser) show significantly reduced AMH protein secretion in vitro.
source: All three of mutations tested (p.Pro151Ser, p.Asp238Glu, and p.Thr99Ser AMH mutants) showed significantly reduced AMH protein secretion in vitro (Figure 7a and Table 1), as assessed by automated chemoluminescent immunoassay.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from AMH secretion assays in COS-7 cells shown in Figure 7a and Table 1.

claim: AMH overexpression in GN11 cells significantly increases cell migration by 50% compared to mock cells.
source: AMH overexpression (AMH WT) in GN11 cells significantly increased cell migration by 50% when compared with mock cells (Figure 7b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from transwell migration assays shown in Figure 7b.

claim: AMH-dependent induction of GN11 cell motility is prevented when cells are transfected with the p.Pro151Ser, p.Asp238Glu, or p.Thr99Ser mutants.
source: The AMH-dependent induction of cell motility was prevented when the cells where transfected with the mutants identified in KS patients (p.Pro151Ser and p.Asp238Glu) as well as with the mutant found in a nCHH proband (p.Thr99Ser; Figure 7b and Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from transwell migration assays shown in Figure 7b and Table 1.

claim: The p.Thr99Ser AMH variant significantly reduces GnRH secretion in GT1-7 cells compared to AMH WT.
source: The p.Thr99Ser AMH variant significantly reduced GnRH secretion as compared to GT1-7 cells expressing the AMH WT (Figure 7c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from GnRH secretion assays in GT1-7 cells shown in Figure 7c.

claim: AMH treatment significantly increases cell migration of AMHR2 WT-transfected GN11 cells compared to serum-free medium.
source: Consistent with the data shown in Figure 5, AMH treatment significantly increased cell migration of AMHR2 WT-transfected cells as compared with SFM (Figure 7d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from transwell migration assays shown in Figure 7d.

claim: The AMHR2 p.Gly445_Leu453del mutant significantly impairs AMH-induced GN11 cell migration.
source: This effect was significantly impaired when GN11 cells were transfected with the AMHR2 mutant plasmid (Figure 7d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from transwell migration assays shown in Figure 7d.

claim: AMH stimulates GnRH secretion in GT1-7 cells expressing AMHR2 WT.
source: These experiments revealed that AMH (50 ng/ml) stimulates GnRH secretion into medium of GnRH cells expressing the AMHR2 WT, whereas introduction of the AMHR2 mutant variant into GT1-7 cells significantly reduced the AMH-dependent GnRH secretion as compared to control conditions (Figure 7e).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from GnRH secretion assays in GT1-7 cells shown in Figure 7e.

claim: The AMHR2 p.Gly445_Leu453del mutant significantly reduces AMH-dependent GnRH secretion in GT1-7 cells.
source: These experiments revealed that AMH (50 ng/ml) stimulates GnRH secretion into medium of GnRH cells expressing the AMHR2 WT, whereas introduction of the AMHR2 mutant variant into GT1-7 cells significantly reduced the AMH-dependent GnRH secretion as compared to control conditions (Figure 7e).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from GnRH secretion assays in GT1-7 cells shown in Figure 7e.

claim: The AMHR2 p.Gly445_Leu453del deletion may result in alterations in intracellular signaling.
source: In summary, although AMHR2 mutant tertiary structure is expected to be folded in a similar manner to that of the WT species, it is possible that the deletion results in some alterations in the intracellular signaling.
evidence: This is based on computational modeling data showing differences in dynamic behavior between WT and mutant AMHR2 shown in Figure 7f-i.

claim: AMH and AMHR2 were originally identified in the mesenchyme of Müllerian ducts and in gonads.
source: Originally identified in the mesenchyme of Müllerian ducts and in gonads (Josso et al., 1998), Amh and Amhr2 were subsequently documented in several other organs, including the brain (Lebeurrier et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2009; Cimino et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2005) and the pituitary (Garrel et al., 2016), suggesting that Amh biological effects could be much broader than initially thought.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation to Josso et al., 1998.

claim: Amh and Amhr2 have been documented in the brain and pituitary.
source: Originally identified in the mesenchyme of Müllerian ducts and in gonads (Josso et al., 1998), Amh and Amhr2 were subsequently documented in several other organs, including the brain (Lebeurrier et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2009; Cimino et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2005) and the pituitary (Garrel et al., 2016), suggesting that Amh biological effects could be much broader than initially thought.
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies documenting expression in these tissues.

claim: Migratory GnRH neurons and developing vomeronasal/olfactory axons express Amhr2 in mammals.
source: We have recently shown that migratory GnRH neurons and developing vomeronasal/olfactory axons express Amhr2 in mammals (Cimino et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors (Cimino et al., 2016).

claim: Amh acts as a promotility factor for GnRH neurons by signaling via Amhr2/Bmpr1b and activation of the MAPK pathway.
source: Moreover, in this study, we showed that Amh acts as a promotility factor for GnRH neurons by signaling via Amhr2/Bmpr1b and activation of the MAPK pathway.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from receptor knockdown and MAPK inhibition experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Amh signaling contributes to the correct development of the ventral branch of the vomeronasal/terminal nerves in the brain through a paracrine mechanism.
source: Since Amh is only produced by GnRH neurons in the fetal brain and because the axonal scaffold of GnRH neurons express Amhr2, we hypothesize that Amh signaling contributes to the correct development of the ventral branch of the vomeronasal/terminal nerves in the brain through a paracrine mechanism.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the expression pattern of Amh and Amhr2 and the observed phenotypes in Amhr2-deficient mice.

claim: Mono-allelic inactivation of Amhr2 in mice is not sufficient to significantly alter GnRH neuronal migration.
source: Mono-allelic inactivation of Amhr2 in mice is not sufficient to significantly alter GnRH neuronal migration, as indicated by the normal number of GnRH neurons observed in adult Amhr2 heterozygous brains.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing no difference in GnRH cell number between Amhr2+/+ and Amhr2+/- mice in Figure 4i.

claim: The presence of only one Amhr2-null allele is sufficient to trigger significant impairments of LH secretion, LH pulsatility and fertility in adult female mice.
source: On the other hand, the presence of only one Amhr2-null allele is sufficient to trigger significant impairments of LH secretion, LH pulsatlity and fertility in adult female mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing reduced LH levels, LH pulse frequency, and fertility in Amhr2+/- females in Figure 4j, 4m, and 4n.

claim: In heterozygous Amhr2+/- males, sexual behavior but not fecundity is likely altered.
source: In heterozygous males, only the number of litters/90 days was found to be significantly reduced as compared to Amhr2+/+ males, suggesting that sexual behavior but not fecundity is likely altered in Amhr2+/- males.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that only litter frequency, not pups per litter, is reduced in Amhr2+/- males.

claim: Bi-allelic inactivation of Amhr2 in mice results in a significant reduction of the GnRH cell population in adult brains of both sexes.
source: Bi-allelic inactivation of Amhr2 in mice results instead into a significant reduction of the GnRH cell population in the brains of adult Amhr2-null mice of both sexes as compared to wild-type animals.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing 40% reduction in GnRH cell number in Amhr2-/- mice of both sexes in Figure 4i and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The GnRH migratory defect observed in Amhr2-deficient embryos is independent of the genetic sex of the animals.
source: Since male and female homozygous adult animals showed a comparable GnRH cell loss, it is likely that the GnRH migratory defect observed in Amhr2-deficient embryos is independent of the genetic sex of the animals.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that both male and female Amhr2-/- mice show similar GnRH cell loss.

claim: Amh/Amhr2 signaling can regulate GnRH migration during embryonic development and GnRH/LH secretion postnatally.
source: We speculate that Amh/Amhr2 signaling can regulate, respectively, GnRH migration, during embryonic development, and GnRH/LH secretion postnatally.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed phenotypes at different developmental stages.

claim: Homozygous Amhr2-/- female mice combine developmental defects in GnRH migration with severely impaired ovulation and fertility in adulthood.
source: Homozygous Amhr2 female mice have a more pronounced phenotype than heterozygous animals, as they combine developmental defects in GnRH migration with severely impaired ovulation and fertility in adulthood.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing GnRH migration defects, reduced corpora lutea, and impaired fertility in Amhr2-/- females.

claim: Part of the reproductive phenotype of Amhr2-/- mice is likely due to the lack of ovarian Amh.
source: Moreover, since Amh is known to be expressed by granulosa cells in the ovaries (Vigier et al., 1984) and to regulate folliculogenesis (Durlinger et al., 2001; Durlinger et al., 1999), it is likely that part of the reproductive phenotype of Amhr2-/- mice is also due in part to the lack of ovarian Amh.
evidence: This is an inference based on established knowledge about ovarian Amh function, supported by citations.

claim: Amh directly increases GnRH and LH secretion.
source: However, our previous (Cimino et al., 2016) and current findings, showing that Amh directly increases GnRH and LH secretion, support a role for Amh in the neuroendocrine regulation of fertility in physiological and pathological conditions.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the current study and citation to previous work (Cimino et al., 2016).

claim: The AMH mutants identified in CHH probands display defects in AMH release.
source: The AMH mutants display defects in AMH release.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from AMH secretion assays in COS-7 cells shown in Figure 7a.

claim: The decreased AMH secretion of the mutants might result from altered protein trafficking leading to accumulation in the endoplasmic reticulum and defective release.
source: Since the described proAMH cleavage sites (Mamsen et al., 2015; Pankhurst and McLennan, 2013) are not located in close proximity of these mutations, it is unlikely that they impinge on the cleavage of the proAMH. The decreased AMH secretion might rather result from altered protein trafficking leading to accumulation of the mutants AMH in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and defective release.
evidence: This is speculation based on the location of the mutations and the observed secretion defects, supported by citations about proAMH cleavage sites.

claim: The AMH mutants identified in KS probands significantly reduce GN11 migration compared to wild-type AMH.
source: The AMH mutants identified in KS probands also significantly reduced GN11 migration compared to the wild-type AMH.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from transwell migration assays shown in Figure 7b.

claim: The p.Thr99Ser AMH mutation compromises both GnRH cell motility in GN11 cells and GnRH secretion in GT1-7 cells.
source: Interestingly, the p.Thr99Ser AMH mutation found in a nCHH proband compromises both GnRH cell motility in GN11 cells as well as GnRH secretion in GT1-7 cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from migration and secretion assays shown in Figure 7b and 7c.

claim: AMH mutants may cause dominant negative effects by forming heterodimers with wild-type AMH.
source: It is plausible that AMH mutants cause dominant negative effects by forming heterodimers with wild-type AMH, thus reducing AMHR2 activation and the downstream biological response.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism by which heterozygous mutations cause a phenotype.

claim: The AMHR2 p.Gly445_Leu453del mutation is loss-of-function in in vitro migration and GnRH secretion assays.
source: Finally, the AMHR2 p.Gly445_Leu453del mutation identified in a female nCHH proband was also loss-of-function in in vitro migration and GnRH secretion assays.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from migration and secretion assays shown in Figure 7d and 7e.

claim: Heterozygous mutations in AMH and AMHR2 are found in 3% of CHH probands (4 out of 136).
source: The heterozygous mutations in AMH and AMHR2 are found in 3% of CHH probands in our cohort (4 out of 136).
evidence: This is based on the number of mutations identified in the cohort.

claim: The mutational prevalence of AMH and AMHR2 in CHH is consistent with the genetic landscape of CHH where the majority of known CHH genes have a low mutational prevalence (<5%).
source: This is consistent with the genetic landscape of CHH as the majority of known CHH genes have a low mutational prevalence (<5%) (Boehm et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Boehm et al., 2015 documenting the genetic landscape of CHH.

claim: Variable expressivity was observed in family members carrying the same AMH or AMHR2 mutation.
source: Variable expressivity was observed in family members carrying the same mutation, consistent with the fact that CHH represents the more severe end of a large spectrum of manifestations.
evidence: This is supported by the pedigree data shown in Figure 6b and 6e.

claim: Factors such as digenic/oligogenic inheritance, epigenetic regulation or non-genetic contributions likely play important roles in CHH phenotype variability.
source: This is a common theme in the genetics of CHH, and factors such as digenic/oligogenic inheritance (Boehm et al., 2015; Sykiotis et al., 2010; Pitteloud et al., 2007), epigenetic regulation or non-genetic contributions likely play important roles.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CHH genetics supported by citations.

claim: Homozygous or compound heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in AMH or AMHR2 cause persistent Müllerian duct syndrome (PMDS) in both mice and humans.
source: Notably, homozygous or compound heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in AMH (OMIM: 600957) or AMHR2 (OMIM: 600956) cause PMDS in both mice and humans (Imbeaud et al., 1995; Mishina et al., 1996).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations to Imbeaud et al., 1995 and Mishina et al., 1996.

claim: PMDS is characterized by the retention of Müllerian duct derivatives in males.
source: PMDS is characterized by the retention of Müllerian duct derivatives (the uterus, fallopian tubes, and upper part of the vagina) in males (Josso and Clemente, 2003; Behringer et al., 1994; Mishina et al., 1996; Belville et al., 1999; Belville et al., 2004; Orvis et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about PMDS supported by multiple citations.

claim: Two mutations (AMH p.Pro151Ser and AMHR2 p.Gly445_Leu453del) identified in the CHH cohort were previously associated with autosomal recessive PMDS.
source: Interestingly, we identified two mutations (AMH p.Pro151Ser and AMHR2 p.Gly445_Leu453del) (Picard et al., 2017) in our CHH cohort previously associated with autosomal recessive PMDS.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Picard et al., 2017.

claim: Monoallelic defects in AMH or AMHR2 do not cause PMDS.
source: MRI or pelvic ultrasounds were performed in the two male CHH patients harboring AMH mutations, including the patient carrying the p.Pro151Ser. No defects in the internal genitalia were identified, consistent with the fact that monoallelic defects in AMH or AMHR2 do not cause PMDS (Picard et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by clinical data from the patients and citation to Picard et al., 2017.

claim: Parents of PMDS probands carrying heterozygote AMH or AMHR2 mutations are fertile.
source: Notably, parents of PMDS probands carrying heterozygote AMH or AMHR2 mutations are fertile (Picard et al., 2017; Josso et al., 2005); however, detailed reproductive and olfactory phenotyping in these parents have not been reported.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Picard et al., 2017 and Josso et al., 2005.

claim: AMH and AMHR2 have pleiotropic roles in shaping internal genitalia and GnRH neuron migration.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate the pleiotropic roles of AMH and AMHR2 in shaping internal genitalia and GnRH neuron migration.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that mutations in these genes cause both PMDS and CHH.

claim: Different mechanistic actions of AMH/AMHR2 mutants in combination with tissue-specific signaling pathways might guide the final phenotype.
source: Different mechanistic actions of the mutants (i.e. recessive vs. dominant negative vs. haploinsufficiency) in combination with tissue-specific signaling pathway might guide the final phenotype.
evidence: This is speculation about how different mutation mechanisms and tissue contexts could lead to different phenotypes.

claim: AMH and AMHR2 mutations affecting GN11 cell motility were found in both KS and nCHH individuals.
source: AMH and AMHR2 mutations affecting GN11 cell motility were found in both KS and nCHH individuals.
evidence: This is supported by the patient data in Table 1 and functional validation in Figure 7.

claim: GnRH migratory defects could occur in some cases of nCHH.
source: We thus speculate that GnRH migratory defects could also occur in some cases of nCHH.
evidence: This is speculation based on the finding of mutations affecting GnRH migration in nCHH patients.

claim: The hypothesis that GnRH migratory defects could occur in nCHH challenges the current dogma that defects in GnRH cell migration lead to KS and not nCHH.
source: This hypothesis challenges the current dogma, whereby defects in GnRH cell migration lead to KS and not nCHH (Boehm et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement about how the findings challenge existing understanding, supported by citation to Boehm et al., 2015.

claim: CHH genes do not segregate into 2 (KS and nCHH) but rather three categories: 1) KS only, 2) nCHH only and 3) both KS and nCHH.
source: Yet, increasing genetic evidence indicates that CHH genes do not segregate into 2 (i.e. KS and nCHH) but rather three categories: 1) KS only, 2) nCHH only and 3) both KS and nCHH.
evidence: This is based on accumulating genetic evidence about CHH gene associations.

claim: Genes involved in GnRH neuron migration such as FGFR1, SEMA7A, and AXL can cause both KS and nCHH.
source: The latter includes genes involved in GnRH neuron migration such as FGFR1, SEMA7A, AXL (Boehm et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Boehm et al., 2015.

claim: GnRH neurons in human fetuses migrate into the brain in tight associations with vomeronasal and terminal nerves and not olfactory nerves.
source: We recently showed that GnRH neurons in human fetuses migrate into the brain in tight associations with vomeronasal and terminal nerves and not olfactory nerves (Casoni et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors (Casoni et al., 2016).

claim: Correct development of the olfactory bulbs and axonal connection to the forebrain are not required for GnRH neuronal migration.
source: Another recent study demonstrated that correct development of the OBs and axonal connection to the forebrain are not required for GnRH neuronal migration (Taroc et al., 2017), thus implying a stronger contribution of the vomeronasal/terminal nerve as a scaffold for the GnRH migration.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Taroc et al., 2017.

claim: The vomeronasal and terminal nerves play important roles in the ontogenesis and migration of GnRH neurons in vertebrates.
source: Taken together, this evidence indicates that the vomeronasal and the terminal nerve play important roles in the ontogenesis and migration of GnRH neurons in vertebrates, and raises the intriguing possibility that some genetic forms of nCHH might be due to defective central projections of the vomeronasal/terminal nerves leading to subsequent alterations of the GnRH migratory process.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited evidence and the findings of the current study.

claim: Some genetic forms of nCHH might be due to defective central projections of the vomeronasal/terminal nerves leading to alterations of the GnRH migratory process.
source: Taken together, this evidence indicates that the vomeronasal and the terminal nerve play important roles in the ontogenesis and migration of GnRH neurons in vertebrates, and raises the intriguing possibility that some genetic forms of nCHH might be due to defective central projections of the vomeronasal/terminal nerves leading to subsequent alterations of the GnRH migratory process.
evidence: This is speculation based on the evidence about the role of vomeronasal/terminal nerves and the findings in nCHH patients.
